Estimate the spatial autocorrelation range from data

Source: R/cross-validation.R
estimate_sac_range.Rd

Fits an exponential variogram model with a nugget and returns the effective range: three times the fitted range parameter, where the semivariance reaches about 95 percent of the sill. Beyond it two observations are close to uncorrelated, so it is the distance a block or a buffer has to exceed. The range is in the units of the projected CRS the variogram is fitted in. Pass it as the block_size of make_folds(), or let make_folds(auto_range = TRUE) estimate it, so that the blocks are at least as wide as the autocorrelation range.

Usage

estimate_sac_range(
  points_sf,
  response_var,
  predictor_vars = NULL,
  n_max = 5000L,
  cutoff = 0.5,
  range_frac = 1,
  seed = 123L,
  detrend = c("ols", "reml"),
  reml_max_n = 400L,
  keep_directional_fits = FALSE,
  lags = c("adaptive", "equal"),
  n_lags = 15L,
  structure_alpha = 0.05
)

# S3 method for class 'sac_range'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

points_sf

An sf layer of points. A lon/lat layer is projected first (spatialkit-geometry); other geometry is reduced to representative points, and Z and M are dropped, since gstat::variogram() would otherwise measure distances in three dimensions. Rows without a location are dropped with a logged count.

response_var

Name of the response column. Rows where it is missing or infinite are left out before anything else is done, so they take no part in the choice of projection for lon/lat input and do not use up the n_max subsample. For a count or other response whose variance tracks its mean, see the section "Count and other non-Gaussian responses": the range is still estimated, but it is less reliable than for a Gaussian response.

predictor_vars

Optional character vector of predictor column names. When given, the trend on these predictors is removed first and the variogram describes the residual autocorrelation, the part a spatial model has to handle once the covariates have done their work. How the trend is removed is set by detrend (see the section "Detrending and the residual-variogram bias"). Rows whose response or predictor is missing or infinite are left out of that fit, and so of the variogram, with a logged count; when that leaves fewer than 30 rows, or fewer than 30 distinct locations, the result is the unclassed NA that says how many were left (see Value). When no row has every predictor (one is missing on every row) no trend can be fitted, and the variogram is of the raw response, with an R warning and detrended set to FALSE. Where nothing is fitted then either (fewer than 30 distinct locations, a constant response, or points with no extent), the result is the NA with its reason, and there is no such warning.

n_max

The most points the variogram is computed on, at least 30; Inf for no limit. Variogram estimation is O(n^2), so this bounds the run time. A layer with more rows that carry a value is cut to a seeded random subsample of this size, drawn after the rows with nothing to model are left out and with the rows in a fixed order, so the subsample does not depend on how the layer is sorted. The counts are returned as the attributes n_used, n_missing and n_subsampled. The floor of 30 distinct locations applies to the rows the variogram is computed on, and a subsample of a layer with many rows a location can hold fewer locations than the layer. When the layer itself has 30 locations or more and the subsample holds fewer, the reason of the NA says "of the n_max subsample", and a larger n_max keeps more of them; when the layer has fewer than 30, the reason gives the layer's counts.

cutoff

Fraction of the largest distance between two points to use as the variogram lag cutoff, above 0 and at most 1. That distance is the farthest pair, found on the convex hull, not the diagonal of the bounding box, which depends on how the axes are oriented. Default 0.5.

range_frac

A positive number, default 1. A fitted range beyond range_frac * cutoff * max_dist (at the default, beyond the longest lag the empirical variogram was fitted over) is treated as unidentified and the result is NA. A model fit gives a finite number even when the variogram never reaches a sill, and such a value extrapolates past the observed lags; passed to make_folds(auto_range = TRUE) it would collapse the block grid to a single block. Raise range_frac to accept ranges extrapolated beyond the fitted lags. The bound does not guarantee room for two blocks: at the defaults it is half the farthest-pair distance, about 0.71 of the side of a square layer, and a block grid needs a range below half the width of the bounding box in one direction or the other. An accepted range between the two leaves make_folds(auto_range = TRUE) room for a single block of that size (see its auto_range argument). Lowering range_frac to fit the grid would turn those estimates into NA and the blocks into geometric ones smaller than the range.

seed

RNG seed for the n_max subsample, the reml_max_n subsample, and the draw of one row a location that detrend = "reml" makes on a layer with repeat visits. With a seed, the caller's random stream is restored afterwards. Default 123, so the same layer gives the same range on every run; NULL leaves the draws unseeded, and another number shows how sensitive the estimate is to the subsample. It has no effect where nothing is drawn. On a layer whose rows crowd onto few locations the subsample can also decide whether 30 distinct locations remain, and so whether a range is estimated at all (see n_max).

detrend

How the trend on predictor_vars is removed; ignored when there are none. "ols" (default) fits it by ordinary least squares and fits the variogram to the residuals, which underestimates the range (see the section "Detrending and the residual-variogram bias"). "reml" fits the trend and an exponential-plus-nugget covariance together by residual maximum likelihood with nlme::gls(), returns the REML range, and attaches the empirical variogram of the REML residuals for inspection. It needs nlme, costs O(n^3) and so runs on at most reml_max_n points, and takes one row a location. When it is not fitted (no nlme), cannot be fitted (the design of the trend cannot be built, as on a factor with one level) or does not converge, the "ols" path runs instead with an R warning that says which. The start of the fit is chosen from the profile REML likelihood on a grid of ranges and nugget proportions, and when more than one start is fitted the fit with the largest log-likelihood is kept.

reml_max_n

A whole number of at least 30, default 400. With detrend = "reml", the trend and covariance are fitted on a seeded random subsample of this many points when the layer has more, and the fitted trend is then removed from every point. The fit takes one row a location: where a location has several rows (repeat visits), one of them is drawn at random under seed, so the nugget fitted is the variance between visits and not that of their minimum or of their mean. Raise it for a better-determined fit at a cubic cost.

keep_directional_fits

TRUE or FALSE, default FALSE. Attach each direction's empirical variogram and fitted model as directional_fits. The four variograms are most of the object's size; the numbers read from them (directional, directional_fitted, directional_status, anisotropy) are attached either way, and plot() draws the all-pairs variogram from its own attribute.

lags

How the lags are binned: "adaptive" (default) or "equal"; see the section "The lags".

n_lags

A whole number from 5 to 100, default 15. With lags = "equal", the number of bins. With lags = "adaptive", the most bins spaced geometrically past the first; fewer are used when that many would hold under 30 pairs each.

structure_alpha

The level of the test for spatial structure, above 0 and at most 1; default 0.05. A layer whose adjusted p-value is not below it gets no range. 1 switches the refusal off; the test is still computed and attached.

x

A sac_range object, for print().

...

Ignored.

Value

A single number, in one of three shapes, each of which behaves as an ordinary number. A range that was fitted, and a range fitted and refused, are of class sac_range; a call that could fit nothing returns an unclassed NA. The attributes and the class do not affect is.na() or is.finite(), so code that tests for a missing range treats all three alike.

Success

A positive effective range in the units of the projected CRS, with the fit attached as attributes:

  • crs: the projected CRS the variogram was fitted in, which gives the unit of the range; max_dist and cutoff_dist: the farthest pair and the lag cutoff.

  • variogram: the empirical variogram, in the units of the response's variance; variogram_model: the fitted model, in gstat's layout, or with detrend = "reml" one built from the REML parameters.

  • lags, lag_boundaries and lag_fallback: the binning behind the result, its upper bin edges, and TRUE when adaptive lags were asked for and the equal-lag result is returned (see the section "The lags").

  • first_lag: the mean separation in the first bin, the shortest lag resolved, from which the nugget is extrapolated; bins_below_range: how many bins lie inside the fitted range (with fewer than three, the split between nugget and structure rests on very little).

  • structures and short_range: how many structures the model has besides the nugget, and the effective range of the short one when there are two (NA otherwise).

  • nugget (the model's nugget variance), nugget_at_bound, nugget_floor, short_lag_semivariance, short_lag_pairs, short_lag_dist, zero_lag_semivariance and zero_lag_pairs: the nugget and the evidence to judge it by, described in sac_nugget(). zero_lag_semivariance is NA and zero_lag_pairs 0 when no location has two rows.

  • structure_p, morans_i and structure_test: the adjusted p-value of the test for spatial structure, Moran's I on the 8 nearest neighbours, and the statistic, z and p for each neighbourhood size.

  • directional: the ranges at azimuths 0, 45, 90 and 135 degrees, named by azimuth, NA where that direction's fit was unusable; directional_status: per azimuth, why a direction is NA in directional: "ok", "over_cutoff" (its range ran past the largest lag fitted), "not_converged" (its fit has no minimum inside the ranges searched) or "no_fit" (a flat variogram, or too few bins); directional_fitted: the range each direction's fit reported, usable or not, so a refused directional range stays recoverable; directional_fits: with keep_directional_fits = TRUE, a list by azimuth of each direction's empirical variogram and fitted model (NULL where there is none), and NULL otherwise; anisotropy: the largest directional range over the smallest; anisotropy_used: always FALSE, since the all-pairs fit is the estimate.

  • detrended: whether the variogram is of the residuals on predictor_vars (TRUE) or of the raw response. A predictor that is not a column is an error, and a detrending fit that fails warns and falls back to the raw response with this set to FALSE. detrend_method: "ols" or "reml" when detrended, NA otherwise. reml: with detrend = "reml", a list with n_used, subsampled, nugget_prop, sigma2, logLik (the REML log-likelihood of the fit kept), logLik_gain (its gain over the same trend with independent errors) and n_fits (the starts fitted); NULL otherwise.

  • n_used, n_missing and n_subsampled: the points the variogram was computed on, the rows left out for a missing response or predictor, and the rows the n_max subsample left out.

Rejected range

NA_real_ when no range is identified. It is classed sac_range as well, so it prints as NA without dumping its attributes, and it carries every attribute of a success (the evidence for the rejection), plus rejected_range (the value that was refused, NA when none was fitted) and rejected_reason, one of:

  • "no spatial structure detected at the nearest-neighbour scale": the test in the section "The test for spatial structure". The model attached is a pure nugget at the variance of the modelled variable, and nothing fitted is handed on.

  • "the empirical variogram is flat: no spatial structure at the lags resolved": no model with a range fits the variogram better than a constant. The model attached is that constant, a pure nugget.

  • "empirical variogram decreases with distance": the semivariance falls over the shorter lags (a net fall of more than 15 percent of the mean semivariance there, weighted by pairs), which is the shape of a periodic, hole-effect structure or of a variance that differs between a dense cluster and the rest of the layer. Sampling noise in the short-lag bins of a small sample can make that fall too.

  • "fitted range exceeds the largest lag fitted": the range is past range_frac * cutoff * max_dist (see range_frac). An unremoved trend ends here when the variogram rises past the fitted lags; a milder trend only lengthens the fitted range and passes, which is what predictor_vars is for.

  • "fitted range is below the shortest lag fitted": too few pairs of points lie inside the range to identify it, because it is shorter than the shortest lag the empirical variogram resolves (first_lag) or, with detrend = "reml", than the distance within which 30 pairs of the points the REML fit used lie, when that is shorter (the REML range is fitted to the point pairs, not to the bins). A structure that short cannot be told from a nugget. range_floor holds the distance the refused range fell short of.

  • "fitted range is non-positive or non-finite".

  • "no variogram model could be fitted: fewer than three lag bins hold point pairs". variogram_model is then NULL and nugget is NA.

The reason names one ground for the refusal, in the order above. attr(attr(range, "variogram_model"), "converged") says one thing more about the model: it is FALSE when the least-squares criterion is still falling at an edge of the ranges searched (a variogram with no sill inside four cutoffs), and the nugget and sill of such a model are that edge and not fitted values. For a model with two structures the flag is that of the equal-lag fit the long range came from: when that fit has no minimum, the long structure's range and partial sill are the edge of its search and the flag is FALSE, although the nugget and the short structure were fitted at the adaptive lags. A model built from REML parameters carries no such attribute. resolution_profile() reads it, and takes no nugget from a model marked FALSE.

No fit

An unclassed NA_real_ when estimation could not be attempted at all, whose one attribute, rejected_reason, says why: "package 'gstat', which the variogram needs, is not installed", "<n> points, fewer than the 30 a variogram range is estimated from", "<n> point(s) with a finite value to model, fewer than the 30 a variogram range is estimated from" (the count is of the whole layer's rows with a value), "<k> distinct location(s) among the <n> point(s) with a finite value to model, fewer than the 30 a variogram range is estimated from" (rows that share a location count once; when the layer has 30 or more locations and the n_max subsample kept fewer, the counts are the subsample's and "of the n_max subsample" stands in place of "with a finite value to model"), "the response is constant", "the residuals on predictor_vars are constant: the predictors explain the response exactly" or "the points have no extent (the largest distance between them is zero or could not be computed)". Nothing is fitted, so none of the other attributes exist: no variogram, variogram_model or rejected_range, which is what tells it from a range that was fitted and refused.

Details

The layer is first tested for spatial structure, and a range the data cannot identify is refused: the answer is then NA, with the reason and the evidence attached (see Value). plot.sac_range() draws the variogram behind the estimate, and sac_nugget() reads its nugget.

What is estimated

The estimate is the omnidirectional (all-pairs) fit of an exponential model with a nugget. Only the exponential family is fitted. On fields smoother than exponential that makes the range long, and blocks sized from it come out larger: they still hold the test points at least the field's range from their training data, which blocks sized from a short range do not. Choosing the family by the smaller weighted sum of squares would correct a spherical field but send exponential fields short, and blocks sized from them smaller than the range.

The model is fitted without iteration. The criterion is gstat's weighted least squares (weights N / h^2) on lags divided by the cutoff. For each trial range the nugget and the partial sill are solved exactly, both kept at or above zero, and the range is found by a search over a logarithmic grid from a quarter of the first lag to four cutoffs, refined in one dimension. There is no start value, no iteration limit and no fit that fails to converge.

The test for spatial structure

A variogram model can be fitted to anything, and on a layer with no structure the fit returns a finite range for a large share of draws. So Moran's I of the modelled variable is computed first, on its 2, 4, 8 and 16 nearest neighbours, each standardised with the moments that fit the variable (those of regression residuals when predictor_vars are given), and the smallest one-sided p-value is multiplied by four. When that adjusted p-value is not below structure_alpha, the result is NA with rejected_reason "no spatial structure detected at the nearest-neighbour scale", a pure-nugget model and no fitted range. The test uses no random numbers, and structure_p, morans_i and structure_test are attached to every classed result. Its power is limited where few neighbours lie inside the range, so a short range on a sparse layer can be refused; structure_alpha = 1 switches the refusal off.

Neighbours tied at the k-th distance, those whose squared distances are within one part in ten million of the k-th's, share its slot's weight equally, as in residual_morans_i(). The graphs then do not depend on the unit or the origin of the coordinates wherever the doubles hold them to better than about one part in 1e8 of the distances between neighbours. Where they do not, and a distance lies past a tie by less than that rounding, the call warns with class "spatialkit_xy_imprecise" (see spatialkit-geometry), as it does for the nearest other location of the short-lag semivariances. The results are those the coordinates as stored give.

Rows that share a location (repeat visits) are one place and not each other's neighbours, so on such a layer the test is made on the means of the locations: it asks whether locations near each other are alike, which a location's own effect, however large, does not answer. With very unequal numbers of visits the p-value is approximate. For the same reason a layer needs 30 distinct locations, not only 30 rows; below that the result is the unclassed NA whose reason gives the count (see Value), and nothing is fitted. Five locations visited 20 times give ten pairs of locations and five means, from which neither a range nor a verdict on structure can be read. Two rows are at one location when both their coordinates are equal to the last bit after the projection, so repeat visits recorded with slightly different coordinates count as separate locations; round the coordinates first to pool them.

The lags

With lags = "adaptive" (the default) the first bin runs from zero to the distance within which the closest max(50, n / 4) pairs of distinct locations lie, and up to n_lags further bins are spaced geometrically from there to the cutoff; a bin holding fewer than 30 pairs is merged with the next. The short lags, which the nugget and a short range are read from, are then resolved at the spacing of the points. With lags = "equal" there are n_lags bins of equal width out to the cutoff, as gstat bins by default. Each is cutoff * max_dist / n_lags wide; a structure shorter than the first of them is counted as nugget, and the range fitted is that of whatever longer structure the layer has. Below about a hundred points neither binning resolves much, and the adaptive bins bring no gain.

The adaptive lags put little weight on the long ones, and a weak, long structure under much noise can be clear at equal lags while the adaptive fit runs past the largest lag. So when the adaptive range is refused as past the fitted lags and the equal-lag fit has a range it would itself return, the result is the equal-lag one, whole, as lags = "equal" gives it, with lags saying "equal" and lag_fallback set to TRUE. Its nugget is then the equal-lag nugget. No other refusal falls back.

Structure at two scales

One structure fitted to lags that resolve the spacing of the points follows the shortest structure of the layer. A layer can have a weaker structure several times longer as well, and blocks sized from the short one would leave the long one across folds. So with lags = "adaptive" the equal-lag fit is made too, and when its range is at least twice the adaptive one, a model with a nugget and both structures, at those two ranges, is fitted to the adaptive variogram. That model is returned (structures is 2 and short_range holds the range of the short structure) and the range is the long one, unless the long structure carries under 3 percent of the model's semivariance at the largest lag; then the single structure stands.

The bar is low because the two mistakes are not alike. A long structure that is missed is lost: the range returned is the short one alone. One that is believed in error returns the equal-lag range, which is too long, and short_range still holds the short one. When the equal-lag range is one that lags = "equal" would itself refuse (past the fitted lags, as under an unremoved trend), the model with it is refused as well, the answer is taken away and not lengthened, and the long structure has to carry 10 percent. The nugget comes from the adaptive lags either way. A long structure whose equal-lag range is under twice the adaptive one is not separated: the range is then that of the single fit, which lies between the two.

Directional ranges and anisotropy

Directional variograms are fitted as well, at azimuths of 0 (north-south), 45, 90 (east-west) and 135 degrees, each with a tolerance of 22.5 degrees either way. Those four windows tile all 180 distinct azimuths once, and their ranges are returned in the directional attribute, with their largest-over-smallest ratio in anisotropy. They are a diagnostic and never the answer, for two reasons. Each direction sees about a quarter of the point pairs, and the maximum of four quarter-sample fits is biased upward. And the windows are fixed to the coordinate axes, so any answer built from them changes when the layer is rotated, which a property of the field must not do. The all-pairs fit is the best-powered estimate available and does not change under rotation. When it identifies no range, no range is returned: the largest directional range does not stand in for it.

A direction whose variogram is flat or has too few bins, whose range runs beyond the longest fitted lag, or whose fit has no minimum inside the ranges searched is left out and recorded as NA in directional.

Where a field is known to be anisotropic and blocks are to be at least as large as its autocorrelation range in every direction, size them from the longest directional range yourself. Read it from directional_fitted, not directional: on a strongly anisotropic field the major axis is the direction most likely to run past the fitted lags, which leaves it NA in directional, so max() of that is NA, or with na.rm = TRUE the second-longest range. Check directional_status first: a major axis marked "over_cutoff" has no identified range at all, and a longer cutoff or make_folds(method = "nndm") is the way on. A ratio above 1.5 is written to the package log at INFO level with that advice, which reaches the session log file but not the console (the ratio passes 1.5 on most isotropic fields too).

The nugget

The model is fitted with a nugget. A nugget-free model forces the curve through the origin, and on a measurement that has a nugget the N / h^2 weights buy that constraint by collapsing the range. The fitted nugget can sit at its lower bound of zero; the result then carries nugget_at_bound = TRUE, and sac_nugget() lists what else is attached to judge a nugget by.

Two rows at one location are a pair at zero separation and are in no bin, whichever the binning, since the variogram and the model describe positive separations. Their semivariance, the variance between visits to a location, is returned on its own as zero_lag_semivariance. The nugget fitted to the variogram is not let under it when the layer has 30 or more rows beyond one a location to estimate it from; a model from detrend = "reml" takes no such floor.

Detrending and the residual-variogram bias

Fitting a variogram to the residuals of a least-squares trend underestimates both the sill and the range, because the trend fit absorbs part of the long-wavelength spatial variation (Lark, Cullis and Welham 2006). Blocks sized from that range are then narrower than the field's range, and hold the test points less far from their training data than range-sized blocks are meant to. How large the effect is depends on how smooth the trend terms are in space and on how many there are: it is small for ordinary covariates and large for trend surfaces in the coordinates. Iterating between a GLS trend fit and a variogram refit (Neuman and Jacobson 1984) recovers only part of it, because the variogram of GLS residuals is biased too. REML fits no variogram to residuals, which is why detrend = "reml" returns its own range estimate. Its price is a single family (exponential with nugget), a cubic cost in n, and a somewhat wider sampling spread. The default is "ols"; a script that detrends on smooth or coordinate-based terms should pass detrend = "reml", or size its blocks with a margin above the range returned, to make up the shortfall. Detrending removes a trend the predictors explain; it does not make an unidentified range identified.

Count and other non-Gaussian responses

The empirical variogram assumes second-order stationarity: a variance that is the same everywhere, so that semivariance depends on separation alone. A count response breaks that assumption by construction, because its variance tracks its mean, and so does any response with a mean-variance relationship (rates, proportions, skewed amounts). On such data the variogram mixes distance-dependence with mean-dependence: where the mean is high the semivariance is inflated whatever the distance, which flattens the curve and can lengthen or shorten the apparent range depending on where the high-mean areas sit.

Detrending on predictor_vars removes the part of the mean the covariates explain, but it does not fix the variance structure: the residuals of an OLS fit to a count still have a variance that tracks the fitted mean. The remedy is a variogram of Pearson residuals from a model in the right family, which this function does not compute. Treat the range from a count response as no more than an order of magnitude, since it can come out long or short, and prefer make_folds(method = "nndm"), which needs no fitted range.

Numerical behaviour

The result is a function of the data alone. The same layer gives the same answer whatever the unit of the response or of the coordinates and whatever the order of its rows, and a change in the last bits of the values changes the answer by about as much.

The rows are sorted by their coordinates as supplied, then by the response and the predictors, before anything else, so the projection chosen for lon/lat input, the n_max subsample and the pair sums do not depend on their order. First coordinates within 1e-7 of the diagonal of the points' bounding box count as one column, sorted by the second coordinate, so a lattice whose first coordinates in one column differ in their last bits after a change of unit or origin gets the same order and the same subsample in each. Rows that share a location are therefore in the order of their values, and no step treats the first of them as special.

The variogram is computed on the standardised variable. A response is called constant only when its standard deviation is under 1e-12 of its largest absolute value, which no change of unit alters, and the values centred on their median and scaled have a standard deviation of at most three units in the last place of that value. Residuals of the predictors are called constant when they are no more than the rounding of the regression, taken on the size of the fit's terms, or three such units of the response, whether or not the floor finds spread in them, as the test for cp of resolution_profile() reads them. So 1e15 plus a spread of 1, stored to an eighth, is not constant, and the residuals of a response the predictors fit exactly are, on a predictor far from 0 (a northing) as well. A response that loses its spread on the raw values is centred on its median before the predictors are fitted to it and before the test for spatial structure, neither of which changes under a shift; so is a response whose OLS residuals on the raw values lose their spread (1e15 plus 1e5 times a predictor plus a spread of 1, on that predictor).

The test for spatial structure, the semivariances and the REML fit are taken on the response divided by a power of two near its spread. A response near 1e-160 or 1e160, whose squares lie past what doubles hold, then gives the range, the test and the folds it gives in ordinary units. The variogram, the nugget, the short-lag semivariances and the REML variance are returned in the response's units squared, which near 1e160 are Inf and near 1e-160 are subnormal doubles that keep few bits, or 0. A response so far from zero that doubles there are spaced more than a millionth of its standard deviation apart (a standard deviation of 1 at about 1e10, 2^33, or beyond) is read as stored, rounded to that spacing, with a warning of class spatialkit_response_imprecise.

With detrend = "reml" the REML fit reads the coordinates of the rows it uses centred on the middle of their bounding box, divided by its diagonal and rounded to 2^-30 of it, and the response and each numeric predictor centred on the middle of their range on those rows, divided by it and rounded the same way. Its range, coefficients and variance are taken back to the layer's units. Where the REML range is not identified the likelihood is flat, and whether the fit converges or falls back to OLS is set by the last bits of the coordinates, the response and the predictors; in that frame it does not depend on their units or origins. A value within its own rounding noise of the middle of a step, about a billionth of the diagonal or the range, can still fall on either side of it.

Printing

print() shows the effective range as a plain number, and beneath it the directional ranges and their ratio when the directional fit is available. A direction whose fit was unusable is labelled with why (directional_status) and the range its fit reported (directional_fitted) when the object carries them, and unidentified otherwise. A last line names the unit and the CRS the range is a length in (attr(x, "crs"), which for lon/lat input is the projected CRS the estimate chose; for a layer with no CRS, it says the range is in that layer's own coordinate units), and whether the variogram is of the response or of its residuals on predictor_vars (detrended, detrend_method). print() returns x invisibly.

References

Cliff, A. D. and Ord, J. K. (1981). Spatial Processes: Models and Applications. Pion, London.

Lark, R. M., Cullis, B. R. and Welham, S. J. (2006). On spatial prediction of soil properties in the presence of a spatial trend: the empirical best linear unbiased predictor (E-BLUP) with REML. European Journal of Soil Science, 57(6), 787–799. doi:10.1111/j.1365-2389.2005.00768.x

Neuman, S. P. and Jacobson, E. A. (1984). Analysis of nonintrinsic spatial variability by residual kriging with application to regional groundwater levels. Mathematical Geology, 16(5), 499–521. doi:10.1007/BF01886329

See also

sac_nugget() for the nugget behind the estimate, and plot.sac_range() to see the variogram the estimate rests on.

Other spatial autocorrelation: plot.sac_range(), sac_nugget()

Examples

library(sf)
# A Gaussian random field with an exponential covariance: range parameter
# 100, so the true effective range is 3 x 100 = 300, plus a small nugget.
set.seed(9)
n <- 150
xy <- data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(n, 0, 1000), y = 5e6 + runif(n, 0, 1000))
D  <- as.matrix(dist(xy))
xy$z <- as.numeric(t(chol(exp(-D / 100) + diag(0.1, n))) %*% rnorm(n))
pts <- st_as_sf(xy, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632)
r <- estimate_sac_range(pts, response_var = "z")
r                            # the effective range, in metres
#> 292.1814 
#>   directional: 0 deg = 248.1608, 45 deg = 413.7318, 90 deg = 617.9676,
#>                135 deg = 426.588  (ratio 2.49)
#>   in metres of EPSG:32632; variogram of the response itself
attr(r, "directional")       # the four directional ranges
#>        0       45       90      135 
#> 248.1608 413.7318 617.9676 426.5880 
attr(r, "variogram_model")   # the fitted model behind it
#>   model    psill    range
#> 1   Nug 0.000000  0.00000
#> 2   Exp 1.273642 97.39379
attr(r, "nugget_at_bound")   # TRUE: the fit put the nugget at its bound;
#> [1] TRUE
                             # ?sac_nugget says how to read that
attr(r, "structure_p")       # the test for spatial structure
#> [1] 8.510444e-22

# A field whose range the data cannot pin down: the variogram never
# reaches a sill within the lags fitted, so the answer is NA, with the
# refused value and the reason attached.
xy$trend <- sin(xy$x / 400) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.2)
r2 <- estimate_sac_range(st_as_sf(xy, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632),
                         response_var = "trend")
r2
#> NA 
#>   directional: 0 deg = 2672.119 (past the fitted lags),
#>                45 deg = 2672.119 (past the fitted lags),
#>                90 deg = 2672.119 (past the fitted lags),
#>                135 deg = 2672.119 (past the fitted lags)
#>   in metres of EPSG:32632; variogram of the response itself
attr(r2, "rejected_reason")
#> [1] "fitted range exceeds the largest lag fitted"
attr(r2, "rejected_range")
#> [1] 2672.119

# White noise: no structure, so no range.
xy$noise <- rnorm(n)
r3 <- estimate_sac_range(st_as_sf(xy, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632),
                         response_var = "noise")
attr(r3, "rejected_reason")
#> [1] "no spatial structure detected at the nearest-neighbour scale"
